facts.title: Love steps ashore on a shell
facts.body: Botticelli’s Birth of Venus (c. 1485) stages the goddess arriving on a scallop shell, blown by Zephyr toward a waiting Hora. Painted for the Medici circle, it turns classical myth into a Florentine dream of beauty.

facts.title: Venus — modest and monumental
facts.body: Venus stands at the center in a pose echoing classical statues, hair and hands arranging a graceful modesty. Botticelli elongates her form so she seems both fragile and inevitable.

facts.title: Zephyr and Aura — the breath that carries her
facts.body: On the left, the wind god Zephyr clasps Aura; their breath fills the roses and drives Venus toward land. Motion is drawn as air itself.

facts.title: Hora of Spring — ready with a cloak
facts.body: A Hora (season) waits on the right with a flowered mantle to cover Venus. The shore becomes a ritual of arrival and welcome.

facts.title: The scallop as stage
facts.body: Venus rides a giant scallop — a classical and Christian emblem of birth, pilgrimage, and rebirth. Botticelli makes the shell a floating pedestal.

facts.title: Roses riding the wind
facts.body: Pink roses tumble through Zephyr’s breath. In Medici symbolism, roses bind Venus to spring, love, and Florence’s own garden myth.

facts.title: A painted Cyprus
facts.body: The right shore stands in for Cyprus, Venus’s sacred island. Laurel and myrtle edge a world that is half myth, half Tuscan coast.

facts.title: Myrtle for the goddess
facts.body: Myrtle, sacred to Venus, frames the waiting Hora. Botany becomes devotion.

facts.title: Water drawn as pattern
facts.body: Botticelli’s sea is rhythmic V-shaped ripples more than observed waves — a decorative ocean fit for allegory.
